strengths: The paper identifies a genuine gauge ambiguity in class-pose decomposition and proposes a simple, interpretable normalization using Fréchet means.
The presentation is generally clear, with useful diagrams and a coherent connection between canonicalization, symmetry estimation, and pose-OOD detection.
The method is evaluated on both SO(2) image transformations and SO(3) molecular data; the latter is comparatively large-scale and technically ambitious.
The appendix provides substantial architectural, training, and dataset details, and the qualitative canonicalizations are intuitive.
weaknesses: The empirical evaluation is not competitive enough for the central claims: there are essentially no quantitative comparisons against SGM, partial-equivariance methods, or alternative canonicalization and symmetry-estimation baselines. Most comparisons are qualitative, and the OOD experiment reports AUCs without baselines or sufficient protocol details.

All evaluated symmetries are synthetically imposed with known parametric distributions. The molecular conformers are first aligned to a reference using RDKit and then artificially rotated, so describing this as discovery of real-world 3D symmetry distributions overstates the evidence.

The central construction requires a unique, stable Fréchet mean, but this can fail for broad, multimodal, or highly symmetric distributions. This is especially relevant to the approximately free axial rotations used in the SO(3) experiment. The paper claims broad applicability to arbitrary Lie-group distributions without adequately addressing this identifiability limitation.

The theory assumes access to true equivalence classes and an equivariant pose estimator, whereas experiments substitute fixed-size nearest-neighbor sets in a learned latent space. There is no analysis of neighborhood contamination or representation error beyond a small MNIST sensitivity plot, and the convergence result does not justify this practical pipeline.

The SO(3) implementation appears inconsistent with the stated method: the appendix uses the mode of a fitted matrix-Fisher distribution in place of the Fréchet mean and, in one normalization formula, multiplies by the estimated offset rather than its inverse. The equivalence of these operations to Proposition 3.1 is not established.

The 3D results lack precise aggregate distributional metrics, uncertainty across training runs, and strong ablations. Matrix-parameter MSE is difficult to interpret, and the claim that roughly 80% of molecules are accurate relies on a visually selected MSE threshold.

Train/test splits retain conformers from the same molecule classes, and the image tasks retain the same ten semantic classes. Thus the learned inference maps are not shown to recover symmetry distributions for genuinely unseen classes, despite language suggesting generalization to unseen inputs.

The technical novelty is modest: under the strong assumptions, the main result largely formalizes centering pose samples by their Fréchet mean. Given the missing baselines and unresolved identifiability and implementation issues, the current evidence does not establish a top-tier contribution.

The method is evaluated on both SO(2) image data and SO(3) molecular conformations, and the latter is a useful attempt to move beyond the predominantly two-dimensional settings studied previously.
The appendix supplies architectural and training details, and the qualitative canonicalizations clearly illustrate the intended effect of the normalization.
The OOD-pose experiment suggests a plausible downstream use for learned pose distributions.
weaknesses: The central theoretical result is not established under its stated assumptions. The proof invokes uniqueness and local strict convexity of the Fréchet functional, Lipschitz continuity of the Fréchet-mean map in Wasserstein distance, and a right-invariant metric, but Proposition 3.1 does not assume the required support restrictions, curvature conditions, uniqueness, or metric invariance. These issues are particularly consequential on SO(3), where intrinsic means can be non-unique and cut-locus effects matter.

The implementation does not cleanly match the theory. In the SO(3) experiment, the alleged Fréchet mean is estimated as the mode of a fitted matrix-Fisher distribution, although the paper explicitly distinguishes modes from Fréchet means. Appendix C.2.4 also writes the normalized rotations as ψ(x)Γ rather than ψ(x)Γ^{-1}. Thus the main guarantee does not directly cover the reported 3D procedure.

The empirical evidence is substantially weaker than the claims. All pose distributions are synthetically imposed: MNIST/FashionMNIST use label-dependent rotations, while GEOM conformers are first externally aligned and then assigned one of only three artificial matrix-Fisher distributions. This does not demonstrate discovery of unknown symmetries naturally present in real 3D data.

The GEOM split contains conformers from the same 2,221 molecule identities in training, validation, and test. Since each molecule is randomly assigned a distribution independently of molecular structure, an invariant predictor can succeed by memorizing molecule identity. There is no evaluation on unseen molecules, so the claimed generalization to unseen inputs and instance-specific symmetry inference is not convincingly established.

There are effectively no quantitative comparisons against competing methods or even simple baselines. SGM and IE-AE receive only qualitative comparisons, and the paper omits oracle-label neighborhoods, direct k-NN estimation, unnormalized predictors, alternative centering rules, and adaptations of SGM. Consequently, it is unclear whether the proposed machinery improves on elementary post-processing.

The evaluation reports one fixed seed without uncertainty, provides few exact numerical results, and uses an unexplained matrix-parameter MSE whose threshold for an 'accurate' prediction is chosen visually. The claim that roughly 80% of molecules are accurate is therefore not rigorous. The OOD AUC results likewise lack baselines, uncertainty, and sufficient protocol details.

The practical k-nearest-neighbor construction is not the equivalence class used by the theory. The paper provides no neighborhood-purity or latent-space retrieval evaluation, while its sensitivity plot already shows worsening performance as k grows. This leaves a core dependency of the method insufficiently validated.

The contribution is technically modest: once equivariant pose estimates and suitable same-class neighbors are available, right-centering them by an empirical group mean is a straightforward gauge-fixing operation. Given the missing baselines and gaps between the theorem, implementation, and evaluation, the evidence does not support acceptance at a top-tier venue.

strengths: The paper identifies a genuine limitation of class-pose decomposition: learned canonical orientations are arbitrary, making pose distributions difficult to interpret or compare across classes.
Fréchet-mean normalization is simple, geometrically motivated, and yields intuitive identity-centered symmetry descriptors and natural-pose canonicalizations.

Extending the framework from SO(2) images to SO(3) molecular graphs is ambitious and technically interesting. The qualitative results suggest that the method can recover useful pose patterns in both settings.
The manuscript is generally clear and well organized, with helpful illustrations and extensive implementation details covering architectures, optimization, and dataset construction.
The OOD-pose detection experiment demonstrates a plausible downstream use of the recovered distributions.
weaknesses: The evaluation lacks quantitative comparisons against the most relevant alternatives, including SGM, Partial G-CNNs, VP G-CNNs, and simpler centering or density-estimation baselines. Qualitative comparisons to IE-AE/SGM do not establish a competitive advantage.

All evaluated symmetries are synthetically imposed. In the molecular experiment, conformers are explicitly aligned to a reference and then rotated using one of three artificial matrix-Fisher distributions. This does not substantiate the broad claims about discovering intrinsic symmetries in real-world 3D data.

The molecular split contains conformers from the same 2,221 molecule classes in training and testing, while each molecule is randomly assigned a distribution. Consequently, the predictor can identify or memorize seen molecules and their random assignments; generalization to unseen molecule classes is not demonstrated.

Proposition 3.1 omits assumptions required by its proof, including uniqueness of the Fréchet mean, support within an appropriate geodesically convex region, and use of a right-invariant metric. The claim is stated for general Lie-group distributions, although the invoked continuity of the Fréchet-mean map does not hold in that generality.

The SO(3) implementation does not clearly match the proposed theory: it estimates the Fréchet mean using the mode of a fitted matrix-Fisher distribution, although a mode is not generally a Fréchet mean. The appendix also writes the normalized rotations as ψ(x)Γ̂ rather than ψ(x)Γ̂^{-1}, contradicting the proposition and Algorithm 1.

Results are reported for a single seed without uncertainty estimates or statistical testing. The molecular threshold for an 'accurate' prediction is selected informally from visualizations, and the parameter-space MSE is not contextualized by meaningful baselines.
The OOD experiment omits important protocol details, sample counts, uncertainty, and baseline detectors. Its AUC values therefore provide limited evidence for the claimed practical utility.

Overall, the normalization idea is promising, but the limited novelty of mean-centering combined with substantial theoretical qualifications and an insufficient comparative evaluation leaves the submission below the top-tier acceptance threshold.

strengths: The paper identifies a genuine limitation of class-pose decompositions: learned canonical orientations are arbitrary and can obscure comparisons between pose distributions.

RECON is conceptually simple and potentially useful. Estimating a neighborhood-dependent pose offset and removing it by group multiplication is compatible with different class-pose backbones in principle.

The experiments cover both SO(2) images and SO(3) molecular conformations, and the 2D test-time canonicalization results are substantial: 92.94% versus 66.90% without canonicalization on rotated MNIST, and 80.32% versus 57.52% on rotated FashionMNIST.

The presentation is generally clear, with an intuitive motivation, explicit algorithm, theoretical discussion, implementation details, computational costs, and acknowledgment of limitations in natural scenes.
weaknesses: The central notion of a “natural pose” is not identifiable from unlabeled data without an additional convention. The paper defines it to be the Fréchet center of the observed pose distribution and then recovers that center. This is a useful gauge-fixing convention, but it does not establish that the resulting orientation is semantically natural; the favorable upright image results rely on synthetically generated distributions already centered at the conventional upright pose.

The manuscript repeatedly describes pose or augmentation distributions as intrinsic “symmetries.” These are different concepts: a distribution over observed transformations need not describe transformations under which an object or task is symmetric. Consequently, several claims about unsupervised symmetry discovery are stronger than what the method and experiments establish.

The 3D evaluation has a serious generalization confound. Train, validation, and test sets contain conformers of the same 2,221 molecule identities, and each molecule is randomly assigned one of only three synthetic matrix-Fisher distributions. An invariant predictor can therefore learn or memorize the molecule-to-distribution assignment. Evaluation on held-out molecule identities, including identities with previously unseen pose distributions, is needed to support instance-level inference or data-efficiency claims.

Despite being presented as a real-world 3D demonstration, the relevant SO(3) signal is synthetically imposed after RDKit alignment. The experiment therefore does not demonstrate discovery of naturally occurring molecular orientation preferences. Moreover, the claimed accurate region of MSE < 800 and the statement that roughly 80% of molecules are accurate are based on visual judgment rather than a principled metric or baseline.

The theoretical proposition omits important conditions from its statement, including uniqueness and local convexity of the Fréchet mean and the right-invariance of the metric used for the translation argument. These are not mild technicalities for broad, multimodal distributions on general Lie groups.

There is a theory-to-implementation mismatch. The theory uses an intrinsic Fréchet mean under squared geodesic distance, whereas the SO(3) implementation estimates a matrix-Fisher mode using SVD/moment matching; these are not generally the same estimator. The claim that the SO(2) Fréchet mean is equivalent to the circular mean is also not generally valid. Thus Proposition 3.1 does not directly justify the implemented method.

The proposed Tukey-Fréchet extension is not supported by a consistency or uniqueness result. For equally weighted multimodal distributions it can have multiple minima, and selecting one through a common initialization is an arbitrary convention rather than convergence to a uniquely defined principal mode. It also appears not to be used in the main experiments.

The empirical comparisons are inadequate for a top-tier claim. Quantitative symmetry-recovery comparisons are largely absent; SGM is shown only qualitatively, and relevant partial-equivariance, canonicalization, or oracle alternatives are not evaluated. The downstream OOD comparison is only against the uncentered version of the same IE-AE pipeline.

Experiments apparently use one fixed seed and provide no repeated-run uncertainty. Important choices such as k=25 and hyperparameters are selected by validation performance, but sensitivity is limited to one MNIST plot. There are no ablations isolating neighborhood quality, pose-estimation error, offset prediction, density prediction, or backbone choice.

The “without retraining” characterization is potentially misleading: the downstream classifier is frozen, but RECON still requires training an expensive IE-AE and two additional predictors on the target data, reportedly taking up to 7.5 A100-days. Architecture agnosticism is asserted but tested with only an IE-AE backbone.

The GEOM downstream task is insufficiently specified, including the exact prediction target and class construction. Its canonicalization gain is also modest—55.7% versus 52.4% without canonicalization—and far below the reported 97.01% perfect-canonicalization reference, weakening the broad practical claim.

strengths: The paper identifies a genuine gauge ambiguity in class-pose decompositions and proposes a simple, intuitive pose-centering correction based on Fréchet means.
The presentation is generally clear, with useful visualizations and extensive implementation details.
The experiments span SO(2) image data and SO(3) molecular data, and consider both symmetry estimation and downstream uses such as pose-OOD detection and test-time canonicalization.
The image experiments show sizable improvements over the unnormalized IE-AE baseline, particularly for test-time canonicalization.
weaknesses: The main proposition is not valid under its stated assumptions. Its proof requires uniqueness and local Lipschitz continuity of the Fréchet mean, support inside an appropriate geodesically convex region, and a suitable right-invariant metric. None is assumed. Broad, uniform, or symmetric multimodal distributions on SO(2) or SO(3) can have non-unique means, precisely in regimes relevant to symmetry discovery.

The claimed recovery of a 'natural' pose is partly definitional: the target distribution is defined to have its Fréchet mean at the identity. Without external orientation information, semantic natural orientation remains gauge-unidentifiable. Centering relative poses is useful, but it does not by itself recover an independently defined true canonical pose.

The robust Tukey-Fréchet extension is disconnected from the central guarantee and main experiments. It can have multiple local optima, depends on an initialization and threshold, and is claimed to select a consistent mode without a corresponding theorem. The SO(3) experiment instead uses the mode of a fitted matrix-Fisher distribution rather than the proposed empirical Fréchet estimator.

The evaluation does not convincingly establish instance-specific symmetry discovery. MNIST and FashionMNIST use only a few class-conditioned synthetic rotation distributions, so recognizing the class and predicting its fixed parameter is sufficient. GEOM similarly assigns one of only three synthetic distributions to each molecule.

The GEOM split is especially problematic: conformers from each molecule are divided across training, validation, and test sets, while the molecule's rotation distribution is randomly assigned. The model can therefore memorize molecule identity and its assigned distribution. There is no held-out-molecule evaluation, and the setup cannot demonstrate generalization to unseen classes.

Baselines are inadequate. Most comparisons use only the underlying unnormalized IE-AE, despite related symmetry-learning methods being discussed. The downstream study omits standard alternatives such as augmentation, test-time averaging, equivariant classifiers, PCA or geometry-based alignment, and other learned canonicalizers.

Empirical reporting is weak: results appear to use one fixed seed, uncertainty is absent, several plots lack numerical summaries, and the claim that roughly 80% of molecules are accurate relies on a visually selected MSE threshold. The GEOM canonicalization gain over no canonicalization is only 55.7% versus 52.4%, far below the reported 97.0% perfect-canonicalization reference.

Claims such as architecture-agnostic, retraining-free, robust, and the first 3D symmetry discovery demonstration are stronger than the evidence. The method requires training a specialized class-pose autoencoder and two additional predictors, with multi-day computation; only the downstream classifier avoids retraining. Code is merely promised, further limiting current reproducibility.

strengths: The core idea is simple, intuitive, and useful: estimating the canonical-pose offset from neighboring relative poses and removing it by right multiplication produces substantially more interpretable, data-aligned canonicalizations.

The paper addresses a meaningful limitation of class-pose decomposition methods and connects symmetry discovery to practical applications, including pose-OOD detection and test-time canonicalization of frozen classifiers.

The experimental scope is broader than is typical for this topic, covering SO(2) image transformations and SO(3) molecular conformations, with sizeable 3D experiments and detailed implementation information.

The reported improvements are substantial in the strongest image results: RECON raises rotated-MNIST accuracy from 66.90% to 92.94% and rotated-FashionMNIST accuracy from 57.52% to 80.32%, while also improving OOD AUC across all three datasets.

The manuscript is generally clear, visually effective, and appropriately discusses limitations involving object-centric scenes, neighborhood construction, density estimation, and the need to predefine the group.
weaknesses: Proposition 3.1 is stated too broadly. Its proof additionally relies on a unique Frechet mean, support inside a geodesically convex region, a suitable right-invariant metric, and continuity or Lipschitz stability of the mean. These conditions do not hold for arbitrary distributions on arbitrary Lie groups but are absent from the proposition.

The robust Tukey-Frechet extension is under-justified. For symmetric multimodal distributions it has multiple equivalent minima, so initialization determines which mode is selected; the claim that it consistently converges to the same or principal mode is therefore not established. No downstream experiment evaluates this extension.

The empirical comparison set is weak. The paper primarily compares against raw IE-AE outputs, despite discussing SGM, learned canonicalization, partial-equivariant models, frame averaging, and other symmetry-discovery methods. Comparisons with test-time augmentation or direct pose-estimation baselines are also missing.

Most symmetries are synthetically imposed using known class-dependent distributions. In GEOM, conformers of each molecule occur across training and test splits, so the experiment evaluates new conformers of known molecule identities rather than generalization to unseen molecules. This weakens the claims of real-world and instance-specific symmetry discovery.

Several important results lack rigorous statistical reporting: experiments use one fixed seed, confidence intervals are absent, the 3D claim that roughly 80% of molecules are accurate uses a visually selected MSE threshold, and distributional errors are measured through parameter MSE rather than a divergence between matrix-Fisher distributions.

There is a gap between theory and implementation in the SO(3) experiment: the method is derived using an intrinsic Frechet mean, whereas the implementation estimates a matrix-Fisher mode through SVD/moment matching. The appendix also describes normalization using the centering rotation rather than its inverse, creating ambiguity about the implemented convention.

The broad claim of architecture-agnostic, retraining-free invariance is overstated. Although the downstream classifier is frozen, RECON requires training a computationally expensive group-specific IE-AE and two auxiliary predictors; moreover, GEOM accuracy improves only from 52.40% to 55.70%, far below the 97.01% perfect-canonicalization reference.

Reproducibility is not yet sufficient for acceptance: code is only promised upon publication, hyperparameter selection is incompletely specified, and the downstream GEOM classification target is not clearly described.

strengths: The paper presents a clear and useful gauge-fixing intuition: arbitrary class-pose canonicals can be aligned by estimating a group-space centroid and applying a right translation.
The method is practically motivated, supports SO(2) and SO(3), and produces promising improvements for test-time canonicalization of frozen classifiers.
The experiments include useful analyses of neighborhood size, latent-space neighbor quality, computational cost, stabilizer ambiguity, and multimodal pose distributions.
The manuscript is generally well organized and provides substantial architectural and training detail.
weaknesses: The empirical evidence is almost entirely based on synthetically imposed rotations. Even the molecular experiment first aligns conformers and then applies one of only three artificial matrix-Fisher distributions, so it does not substantiate the stronger claims about discovering unknown real-world intrinsic symmetries.

Generalization is evaluated on new samples from the same digit or molecular identities used in training. In GEOM-QM9, train, validation, and test conformers share the same 2,221 molecules, and each molecule is assigned one of three distributions; consequently, the predictor can learn an identity-to-distribution mapping rather than discover symmetries for unseen classes.

The theoretical equivalence classes and implemented neighborhoods do not match. The proposition assumes i.i.d. samples from a true equivalence class defined through epsilon-connected components, whereas the algorithm uses a separate fixed-k neighborhood for every input. No result controls contamination, class recovery, or the effect of this approximation, although it is central to the method.

The main convergence proposition relies on uniqueness and local convexity of the Frechet mean, support within an appropriate geodesic ball, an invariant metric, and effectively exact equivariance. These important conditions are not fully stated in the proposition and can fail for the multimodal or stabilizer-rich cases emphasized by the paper.

The proposed Tukey-Frechet extension does not generally select a unique or consistent mode for symmetric multimodal distributions; its result depends on initialization. It is supported only by illustrative simulations and is not evaluated in the main downstream experiments.

The comparison protocol uses test accuracy to choose hyperparameters for EquiAdapt and the equivariant baselines, creating test-set leakage and weakening the claimed comparative advantage. Several results, especially on GEOM-QM9, also appear to use a single seed despite reporting near-zero uncertainty.

The downstream evidence is incomplete: OOD detection uses constructed pose anomalies and only an uncentered IE-AE baseline, while the GEOM-QM9 classification target is not clearly specified. Broader OOD baselines, natural shifts, and rigorous multi-seed evaluation are missing.

Calling the inference module 'plug-and-play' and 'retrain-free' is overstated. Although the frozen downstream classifier is not retrained, the approach requires a domain-specific IE-AE plus two additional predictors, with reported training taking roughly 7.5 days for the molecular setting.

Overall, the core normalization operation is relatively simple, and the current synthetic, partially leaked evaluation does not provide sufficient evidence that it constitutes a robust instance-specific symmetry-discovery method competitive at a top-tier conference.

strengths: The core gauge-normalization insight is intuitive and potentially useful: estimating and removing the class-dependent pose offset makes distributions from arbitrary class-pose canonicalizations more comparable and interpretable.
The paper considers both SO(2) image experiments and SO(3) molecular data, and demonstrates applications to pose-OOD detection and test-time canonicalization.
The appendices provide substantial implementation detail, computational measurements, neighborhood-size studies, and analysis of nearest-neighbor class quality.
weaknesses: The main proposition is overstated. It is presented for a general Lie group but the proof additionally needs a right-invariant metric, uniqueness of the Fréchet mean, support within an appropriate geodesically convex region, and continuity or stability of the mean map. These conditions are not in the proposition and fail for important multimodal or symmetric distributions. The proof also assumes exact equivariance of the learned pose estimator without accounting for approximation error.

The claimed robust Tukey-Fréchet contribution is disconnected from the actual experiments: the implementations use a circular mean for SO(2) and a fitted matrix-Fisher mode for SO(3), not the proposed Tukey-Fréchet estimator. No substantive multimodal experiment or ablation establishes its robustness, despite “robust” being central to the title.

The evaluation is overwhelmingly synthetic. MNIST/FashionMNIST rotations are label-programmed, while GEOM conformers are first externally aligned and then assigned one of only three artificial matrix-Fisher distributions. Thus the work does not demonstrate discovery of naturally occurring, diverse instance-specific symmetries in real data.

The strongest instance-specific generalization claim is insufficiently tested: GEOM splits conformers of every molecule across train, validation, and test, so test molecules are not unseen classes and the learned maps may recognize molecule identity. A held-out-molecule evaluation is needed.

There are no strong quantitative symmetry-recovery comparisons against closely related methods such as SGM, Implicit-PDF, or other symmetry-discovery approaches. Downstream comparisons do not substitute for evaluating the central recovery claim, and key ablations—normalization choice, learned mapping versus direct estimation, pose-estimation error, and alternative class-pose backbones—are missing.

The “plug-and-play,” “architecture-agnostic,” and “without retraining” language is misleading. Although the downstream predictor is frozen, RECON requires training an expensive IE-AE and two additional predictors for each domain, taking up to roughly 7.5 A100-days; only an IE-AE-based pipeline is demonstrated. Moreover, the method improves GEOM accuracy only from 52.40% to 55.92%, far below the reported 96.40% ideal canonicalization and 98.55% equivariant model.

Several evaluation practices reduce confidence: EquiAdapt and equivariant baseline hyperparameters are explicitly selected using test accuracy, the number of random runs behind reported uncertainties is unspecified, and the text alternates between fixed-seed deterministic experiments and multiple-seed results.

The notion of a “natural pose” is defined as the center of the observed pose distribution rather than independently identified. It is therefore a gauge convention that can be non-unique or out of support, not generally an identifiable semantic orientation; stabilizers and symmetric objects exacerbate this ambiguity.

strengths: Addresses an important problem: discovering instance-dependent pose distributions and constructing data-aligned canonicalizations without pose or class supervision.
The proposed normalization is simple, intuitive, architecture-agnostic, and potentially useful as a post-processing step for class-pose models.
Evaluation spans SO(2) images and substantially more challenging SO(3) molecular data, with downstream demonstrations in pose-OOD detection and canonicalization for frozen classifiers.
The paper is clearly motivated and generally well written, with helpful visualizations and unusually extensive implementation, computational-cost, neighborhood-size, and latent-neighborhood analyses.

The reported downstream gains are practically interesting: RECON substantially outperforms arbitrary IE-AE canonicalization and is competitive with or better than EquiAdapt on FashionMNIST and GEOM-QM9.
weaknesses: The theoretical result is overstated as written. Proposition 3.1 requires assumptions such as a right-invariant metric, existence and uniqueness of the Frechet mean, support within a suitable geodesically convex region, and stability of the mean map; these do not follow merely from the stated assumptions for a general Lie group. Multimodal distributions can directly violate them.

There is a gap between theory and implementation. The proposition assumes i.i.d. samples from the true equivalence class, whereas the algorithm uses a fixed-size k-nearest-neighbor set that can mix classes. Moreover, the SO(3) implementation estimates the mode of a fitted matrix-Fisher distribution rather than the empirical Frechet mean, and the proposed Tukey-Frechet estimator is not covered by the consistency result.

The robust Tukey-Frechet construction can have multiple minima and depend on initialization or tuning parameter c. The claim that it consistently selects the same mode is not theoretically established, so the resulting 'natural pose' may remain arbitrary for symmetric or multimodal data.

All ground-truth symmetry distributions are synthetically imposed. In particular, molecular conformers are first aligned and then artificially rotated using only three matrix-Fisher families. This is a useful controlled test but does not establish discovery of unknown symmetries in naturally occurring, unaligned data, making several real-world claims too strong.

The central operation is essentially centering predicted poses by an estimated group mean. Its conceptual simplicity is attractive, but the paper does not convincingly isolate how much novelty or benefit comes from this step versus the expensive IE-AE backbone, neighborhood construction, and separately trained predictors.

The downstream comparison has methodological concerns: EquiAdapt hyperparameters are explicitly selected using test accuracy, which constitutes test-set leakage. The paper also reports uncertainty intervals while stating that experiments use a fixed seed, without clearly explaining the number and source of repeated runs.

The description of a plug-and-play 'test-time' layer understates the required setup: RECON needs access to a target-domain training collection, a trained IE-AE, pseudo-label computation, and training two additional networks—reported to take roughly 7.5 GPU-days for GEOM. It avoids retraining the downstream classifier, but is not a lightweight test-time-only procedure.

Reproducibility is incomplete in the submitted document: the claimed public-code link and reproducibility statement are effectively blank, and some implementation notation is inconsistent, including whether the SO(3) normalization multiplies by the centering rotation or its inverse.
